For I will set dung upon my head and will weep and pray that Yahuah (Lord) will hearken to me and send his angel (and bring me a plant from paradise), and I will bring it thee that thy trouble may cease from thee.' Seth saith to him: 'And how hath this come upon thee'* (Adam and Eve 6:1) Seth is ready to go and bring the fruit, but Moses has already told why no son of Adam can simply go for it. Moses records the word of Yahuah Elohim (the LORD God) to Adam himself, and it lays the weight on the man as well, because he hearkened and he ate.

But the devil went to Adam's lot, where the male creatures were. [For Elohim (God) divided the creatures; all the males he gave to your father and all the females he gave to me.]* (Adam and Eve 15:1) Eve tells her children that she and Adam were guarding paradise, each in an allotted portion. Moses says it more briefly: Yahuah Elohim (the LORD God) put the man in the garden to dress it and to keep it. The keeping was given to the man as work, and this book remembers it as a watch.

cards.note: Genesis 3:1 — *Now the serpent was more subtil than any beast of the field which Yahuah Elohim (the LORD God) had made. cards.note: Deuteronomy 4:9 — *Only take heed to thyself, and keep thy soul diligently, lest thou forget the things which thine eyes have seen, and lest they depart from thy heart all the days of thy life: but teach them thy sons, and thy sons’ sons;* *Now then, my children, I have shown you the way in which we were deceived; and do ye guard yourselves from transgressing against the good.'* (Adam and Eve 30:1) Eve ends her telling by warning her children and her children's children to guard themselves. cards.note: Ezekiel 1:1 — *Now it came to pass in the thirtieth year, in the fourth month, in the fifth day of the month, as I was among the captives by the river of Chebar, that the heavens were opened, and I saw visions of Elohim (God).* *Then Seth arose and came to his mother and to her he saith: 'What is thy trouble Why weepest thou' (And) she saith to him: 'Look up and see with thine eyes the seven heavens opened, and see how the soul of thy father lies on its face and all the holy angels are praying on his behalf and saying: 'Pardon him, Father of All, for he is Thine image." 'Pray, my child Seth, what shall this mean And will he one day be delivered into the hands of the Invisible Father, even our Elohim (God) But who are the two negroes who stand by at the prayers for thy father Adam'* (Adam and Eve 35:1) Eve tells Seth to look up and see the seven heavens opened. threads.title: Seth offers to fetch the fruit of paradise
threads.summary_md:
Adam lies sick, and Seth offers to go for the fruit: *I will go and bring thee fruit from paradise* (Adam and Eve 6:1). It is a son's love, and it meets what Moses wrote of that tree: *And Yahuah Elohim (the LORD God) said, Behold, the man is become as one of us, to know good and evil: and now, lest he put forth his hand, and take also of the tree of life, and eat, and live for ever:* (Genesis 3:22) Then Yahuah Elohim (the LORD God) set a guard where the man could not pass: *So he drove out the man; and he placed at the east of the garden of Eden Cherubims, and a flaming sword which turned every way, to keep the way of the tree of life.* (Genesis 3:24) No son of Adam walks back in on his own errand.

It ain't new that the tree of life is held back, and it ain't new who is let in again. The last page of the canon says it plainly: *Blessed are they that do his commandments, that they may have right to the tree of life, and may enter in through the gates into the city.* (Revelation 22:14) The way back to the tree is the way of the commandments, and the gates are opened to those who keep them. The canon sets the tree at the end and the commandments on the road to it.

threads.title: Adam reproves Eve — and the blame that passes across the household
threads.summary_md:
After the beasts turn on them, Adam turns on Eve: *How was thy mouth opened to eat of the tree concerning which Elohim (God) enjoined thee not to eat of it* (Adam and Eve 11:1). The question is fair, and Moses shows how old the habit of the answer is. When Yahuah Elohim (the LORD God) asked, the man said: *And the man said, The woman whom thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I did eat.* (Genesis 3:12) The finger went to the woman, and through her to the One who gave her.

But the word of Yahuah (the LORD) did not stop at the woman. *And unto Adam he said, Because thou hast hearkened unto the voice of thy wife, and hast eaten of the tree, of which I commanded thee, saying, Thou shalt not eat of it: cursed is the ground for thy sake; in sorrow shalt thou eat of it all the days of thy life;* (Genesis 3:17) The man heard, and the man ate, and the sentence on the ground is spoken to him. Eve's mouth was opened, and so was Adam's ear, and neither can be set down as the only cause. Genesis does not hide the woman's part, and it does not let the man stand free of his. This book keeps the argument between husband and wife going, and the canon lets both stand answerable and leaves the way open for both to turn.

threads.title: Guarding paradise, each in the allotted portion
threads.summary_md:
Eve begins the telling of how the enemy deceived them: *we were guarding paradise, each of us the portion allotted to us from Elohim (God)* (Adam and Eve 15:1). The task is old. In Genesis the man was not set in the garden to rest only, but to work it: *And Yahuah Elohim (the LORD God) took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it.* (Genesis 2:15) Dressing and keeping are two halves of one charge, and keeping means watching over.

Eve goes on to say that the creatures were divided between them, the males to Adam and the females to her. Moses does not say that, and the witness itself puts the line in brackets. What Genesis does show is the creatures coming to Adam: *And out of the ground Yahuah Elohim (the LORD God) formed every beast of the field, and every fowl of the air; and brought them unto Adam to see what he would call them: and whatsoever Adam called every living creature, that was the name thereof.* (Genesis 2:19) The dominion over the beasts begins with him, and with that the question of who kept what, and where the keeper was not looking, is already waiting. The scene Eve describes is the watch before the failure of the watch.

threads.title: The devil counsels the serpent
threads.summary_md:
Eve's account opens the door behind the garden scene: *Fear not, only be my vessel and I will speak through thy mouth words to deceive him* (Adam and Eve 16:2). Moses gives us only what was heard, and it is exactly what the vessel would say: *Now the serpent was more subtil than any beast of the field which Yahuah Elohim (the LORD God) had made. And he said unto the woman, Yea, hath Elohim (God) said, Ye shall not eat of every tree of the garden?* (Genesis 3:1) A question was put in the mouth of the serpent, and the question has a speaker.

John gives the speaker his names. *And the great dragon was cast out, that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan, which deceiveth the whole world: he was cast out into the earth, and his angels were cast out with him.* (Revelation 12:9) The old serpent, the Devil, and Satan are one, and he is a deceiver of the whole world. The serpent's fear of Yahuah (the LORD) in this book is one of the places where the retelling adds colour; what Genesis and Revelation hold is steady. The first deception began with a question about what Elohim (God) had said, and it was a spoken thing by one who wanted the man out of the garden. It ain't new that the voice behind the serpent has a name, and that the canon knew him from the first page to the last.

threads.title: Thou art just — the driving out and the plea
threads.summary_md:
They are driven out amid lamentation, and Adam asks for a little space to entreat Yahuah (the Lord). Then Yahuah (the Lord) speaks to the angels, and they fall down and answer: *Thou art just, O Yahuah (Lord), and thou judgest righteous judgement* (Adam and Eve 27:1). Moses tells the driving out without a word of pleading: *So he drove out the man; and he placed at the east of the garden of Eden Cherubims, and a flaming sword which turned every way, to keep the way of the tree of life.* (Genesis 3:24) The cherubim and the sword are the answer the garden gives to the man who ate.

The psalmist says what the angels say, and says it out of his own trouble: *Righteous art thou, O Yahuah (LORD), and upright are thy judgments.* (Psalm 119:137) That is how the canon holds both together, a sentence that is right and an Elohim (God) who hears the one who pleads. Adam does not argue the judgment, he only asks to entreat; and the angels do not argue it either. It ain't new that the judgement is just. What this book adds is the quiet moment in which the first man is heard and not excused.

threads.title: Guard yourselves — the telling handed down
threads.summary_md:
Eve closes the long account of the deception with a word to her descendants: *do ye guard yourselves from transgressing against the good* (Adam and Eve 30:1). The account is for them. In Genesis her own telling is a single line: *And Yahuah Elohim (the LORD God) said unto the woman, What is this that thou hast done? And the woman said, The serpent beguiled me, and I did eat.* (Genesis 3:13) This book lengthens it, and what it is for is made plain by the words that follow.

Moses gives the pattern to Yashar'el (Israel) in the same shape: *Only take heed to thyself, and keep thy soul diligently, lest thou forget the things which thine eyes have seen, and lest they depart from thy heart all the days of thy life: but teach them thy sons, and thy sons’ sons;* (Deuteronomy 4:9) The fathers who saw something are charged to hand it down to sons and sons' sons, so that it will not depart from the heart. It ain't new that a failure is to be told, not buried. The household that passes on how it was deceived is doing what the Torah asks of Yashar'el (Israel), keeping a testimony alive for the next generation, and that is the reason the story is told.

threads.title: The Lord of Hosts comes down to the body of Adam
threads.summary_md:
The archangel asks about the laying out of the remains, and Elohim (God) commands the angels to assemble. Then comes the descent: *the 'Lord of Hosts' came on and four winds drew Him and cherubim mounted on the winds* (Adam and Eve 38:1). The picture is older than this book: *And he rode upon a cherub, and did fly: yea, he did fly upon the wings of the wind.* (Psalm 18:10) The coming of Yahuah (the LORD) on the wings of the wind, with a cherub beneath, is David's song before it is anyone's vision of an angelic funeral.

One man stays awake when the fragrance falls on all the sons of Adam: *Seth alone, because he was born 'according to the appointment of Elohim (God) '* (Adam and Eve 38:1). Moses has the word from the mother's mouth: *And Adam knew his wife again; and she bare a son, and called his name Seth: For Elohim (God), said she, hath appointed me another seed instead of Abel, whom Cain slew.* (Genesis 4:25) It ain't new that the line runs through the appointed one. The canon names Seth as the seed set in the place of Abel, and this book keeps that memory in a single detail: the son who is appointed does not sleep.

threads.title: A booth and seven days of mourning
threads.summary_md:
Driven out of paradise, they build a booth and mourn: *they made themselves a booth, and spent seven days mourning and lamenting in great grief* (Adam and Eve 44:1). Genesis is short about the going out: *Therefore Yahuah Elohim (the LORD God) sent him forth from the garden of Eden, to till the ground from whence he was taken.* (Genesis 3:23) What the man did with his first days outside, Moses does not say, and this book fills the silence with a house of branches and a week of weeping.

The weeping is not left without a direction. Joel hears Yahuah (the LORD) say what such weeping is for: *Therefore also now, saith Yahuah (LORD), turn ye even to me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning:* (Joel 2:12) The call is not to a performance but to a return, with the whole heart. It ain't new that the road out of a garden and the road back both pass through grief. The canon does not make a rule of the booth; it puts beside it the call to turn, and the call is the part that stands.

threads.title: Hunger, and the hope of being recalled
threads.summary_md:
After seven days they are hungry and find nothing. Eve sends Adam to look: *Perchance Yahuah Elohim (the Lord God) will look back and pity us and recall us to the place in which we were before* (Adam and Eve 45:1). The hunger is no accident of the wilderness; it is the sentence at work: *In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread, till thou return unto the ground; for out of it wast thou taken: for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return.* (Genesis 3:19) Bread by sweat was the shape of the new life, and Eve is standing at the first day of it.

But her word is not only about bread. She hopes to be looked back upon, and the psalm gives that hope a footing: *Like as a father pitieth his children, so Yahuah (LORD) pitieth them that fear him.* (Psalm 103:13) It ain't new that pity is the answer of Yahuah (the LORD) to those who fear him. This book leaves the question whether they will be recalled open, as Eve does; the canon says the Father does not wait for them to be worthy of his pity, only for them to turn toward him.

threads.title: Wilt thou slay me — and one flesh
threads.summary_md:
Eve, in her grief, tells Adam that perhaps Yahuah Elohim (the Lord God) would bring him into paradise if she were dead, since it was on her account that he was driven out. His answer is quick: *How is it possible that I should stretch forth my hand against my own flesh* (Adam and Eve 46:2). The answer rests on the first word of the garden, spoken when she was first brought to him: *And Adam said, This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh: she shall be called Woman, because she was taken out of Man.* (Genesis 2:23) What he says of her he says of himself.

Moses gives the reason in the verse after: *Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.* (Genesis 2:24) It ain't new that the two are one. The blame Eve takes on herself, and the blame Adam refused to carry in the garden, meet here in the plain refusal to let the household break. Adam turns the conversation to the one thing left to do, to arise and look for something to live on, that they fail not.

threads.title: What is penitence?
threads.summary_md:
Eve asks what she has never been asked: *What is penitence Tell me, what sort of penitence am I to do* (Adam and Eve 48:1). She fears a labour that is too great to endure, and a promise they will not keep. The Preacher sees that fear and gives it a limit: *When thou vowest a vow unto Elohim (God), defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou hast vowed.* (Ecclesiastes 5:4) A vow made in grief is still a vow, and so Eve is right to be careful.

But the question of how much is not the one David answers. After his own fall he says what Elohim (God) wants: *The sacrifices of Elohim (God) are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O Elohim (God), thou wilt not despise.* (Psalm 51:17) It ain't new that Yahuah (the LORD) looks first at the heart, and at the labour second. This book measures penitence in days in the water and fasting; the Psalm says what the days are meant to carry. A broken spirit is not a feat. It is a heart that has stopped defending itself.

threads.title: The devil leads Eve out of the water
threads.summary_md:
Eve hears, believes, and comes out of the water, trembling from the cold. Then: *the devil raised her up and led her to Adam* (Adam and Eve 53:1). Adam sees them together and weeps, and his cry is the cry of someone who has been here before: *How hast thou been again ensnared by our adversary* (Adam and Eve 53:2). Paul knew the pattern and set it down for the assemblies: *And no marvel; for Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light.* (2 Corinthians 11:14) The helper in this book is the same figure as the light in the letter.

The snare is not a thing the captive undoes alone. Paul speaks of the ones who *recover themselves out of the snare of the devil* (2 Timothy 2:26) and who are taken captive at his will. It ain't new that the deceiver comes as a friend, or that the captive can be recovered. This book sets it in a river with a woman who wanted to keep a promise, and the canon sets it in the assembly with those who hear the truth.

threads.title: Woe unto thee, devil — the rebuke
threads.summary_md:
Eve sees who has led her out, falls on her face, and then cries: *Woe unto thee, thou devil. Why dost thou attack us for no cause* (Adam and Eve 54:1). It is a cry of the weak against the strong, and James knows its place in the walk: *Submit yourselves therefore to Elohim (God). Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.* (James 4:7) Submission comes before resistance, and the fleeing belongs to the one who submits.

Zechariah shows who the rebuke ultimately belongs to: *And Yahuah (LORD) said unto Satan, Yahuah (LORD) rebuke thee, O Satan; even Yahuah (LORD) that hath chosen Jerusalem rebuke thee: is not this a brand plucked out of the fire?* (Zechariah 3:2) It ain't new that the answer to the accuser comes from Yahuah (the LORD) and not from the accused. Eve's words are real and brave, and they are not the last word, for she is not able to send him away herself. The next scene shows the answer, when Adam cries to Yahuah (the Lord) and the devil vanishes.

threads.title: Expelled from my glory — whose fault the fall was
threads.summary_md:
With a heavy sigh the devil speaks to Adam: *it is for thee that I have been expelled from my glory* (Adam and Eve 55:1). Adam answers him as an honest man would, that he has done him no harm. The canon agrees with Adam. Ezekiel's word to the covering cherub gives the cause: *By the multitude of thy merchandise they have filled the midst of thee with violence, and thou hast sinned: therefore I will cast thee as profane out of the mountain of Elohim (God): and I will destroy thee, O covering cherub, from the midst of the stones of fire.* (Ezekiel 28:16) And the verse after names the root: *Thine heart was lifted up because of thy beauty, thou hast corrupted thy wisdom by reason of thy brightness: I will cast thee to the ground, I will lay thee before kings, that they may behold thee.* (Ezekiel 28:17)

This book ties the fall to the creation of Adam, and the prophet ties it to the heart that was lifted up. Yahusha (Jesus) saw it happen: *And he said unto them, I beheld Satan as lightning fall from heaven.* (Luke 10:18) It ain't new that the one who falls blames the one beside him. The devil's pursuit of Adam, in this book, is envy dressed as grievance; in Ezekiel it is plain pride, and no one else is held to answer for it.

threads.title: My life is in thy hands — forty days in the Jordan
threads.summary_md:
When Adam hears the devil, he cries out and prays: *O Yahuah (Lord) my Elohim (God), my life is in thy hands. Banish this Adversary far from me* (Adam and Eve 60:1). The prayer is in the psalms already: *My times are in thy hand: deliver me from the hand of mine enemies, and from them that persecute me.* (Psalm 31:15) The man in the water and the king in his trouble ask the same thing from the same Hand.

The water matters too. Adam stands forty days in the Jordan, and the psalmist, who knows what it is to be overwhelmed, cries: *Save me, O Elohim (God); for the waters are come in unto my soul.* (Psalm 69:1) It ain't new that the one in trouble calls on Yahuah (the LORD) from inside it. The devil vanishes in this book at the moment of the prayer. The canon holds that the prayer of the one who submits is heard, and that the enemy has no standing against a man whose life is in the hands of Yahuah (the LORD).

threads.title: Let not the name be blotted out — the seed that serves
threads.summary_md:
Adam hears the word of Elohim (God) and falls prone, praying: *Cast me not out from Thy presence* (Adam and Eve 70:1). David's prayer in the psalms is the same: *Cast me not away from thy presence; and take not thy holy spirit from me.* (Psalm 51:11) The man who has been cast out once asks not to be cast out again, and asks it for the sake of the name.

Then comes the promise: *there shall not be taken from thy seed for ever the (right) to serve Me* (Adam and Eve 70:2). Isaiah gives the promise its end: *For as the new heavens and the new earth, which I will make, shall remain before me, saith Yahuah (LORD), so shall your seed and your name remain.* (Isaiah 66:22) It ain't new that Yahuah (the LORD) keeps the seed. This book puts the promise in the mouth of the Voice to Adam, and Isaiah puts it at the new heavens and the new earth. The name and the seed are held by the One who made them, and neither is blotted out by the failure of one man.

threads.title: The true Light, the Living Life
threads.summary_md:
Adam throws himself on the earth and adores: *Thou art the true Light gleaming above all light(s), the Living Life, infinite mighty Power* (Adam and Eve 71:2). The psalmist uses the same two words, light and life, for the same One: *For with thee is the fountain of life: in thy light shall we see light.* (Psalm 36:9) The fountain and the light are with Yahuah (the LORD), and the man who sees light sees it in His.

He also says how long this One has been: *Thou art the eternal and supreme Elohim (God)* (Adam and Eve 71:1). The prayer of Moses gives it: *Before the mountains were brought forth, or ever thou hadst formed the earth and the world, even from everlasting to everlasting, thou art Elohim (God).* (Psalm 90:2) It ain't new that the first man worships the One before the mountains. After his worship, the angel Michael seizes his hand and casts him out of paradise, and this book has the waters freeze at the touch of his rod. The praise comes before the leaving, and it does not ask anything back.

threads.title: Seth would go to the gates, and Adam says it is pain
threads.summary_md:
Seth, thinking his father longs for the fruit of paradise, offers to go to the gates: *put dust on my head and throw myself down on the earth before the gates of paradise and lament* (Adam and Eve 74:1). The gesture is old in Yashar'el (Israel): *And Joshua rent his clothes, and fell to the earth upon his face before the ark of Yahuah (LORD) until the eventide, he and the elders of Yashar'el (Israel), and put dust upon their heads.* (Joshua 7:6) Dust and the face to the earth are the body's way of saying that nothing is owed.

Adam says he is not longing for fruit but is in pain, a word Seth does not know. He had not met it. David gives the word its place: *There is no soundness in my flesh because of thine anger; neither is there any rest in my bones because of my sin.* (Psalm 38:3) It ain't new that the flesh carries what the heart has done, and that Yahuah (the LORD) is the One it is brought to. In this retelling the pain is first named to a son who has never felt it, and that is how a father hands down the first lesson of a fallen world.

threads.title: The prohibition, and the portions of paradise
threads.summary_md:
Adam begins his account to his sons, gathered to hear him: *he laid a prohibition on us concerning the tree of knowledge of good and evil, which is in the midst of paradise* (Adam and Eve 75:1). Moses has the same placing: *And out of the ground made Yahuah Elohim (the LORD God) to grow every tree that is pleasant to the sight, and good for food; the tree of life also in the midst of the garden, and the tree of knowledge of good and evil.* (Genesis 2:9) Two trees stand in the middle, and one is to be left alone.

The command comes with a plain consequence: *But of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, thou shalt not eat of it: for in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die.* (Genesis 2:17) It ain't new that the Word spoke clearly before the failure, so that neither of them could say they were not told. This book adds a detail the garden story does not carry, the parts of paradise given to Adam and to Eve, east and north to him, south and west to her. Moses gives the command and the trees and says nothing of portions. What the telling keeps is a father telling his sons, before he dies, what was said and what happened.

threads.title: Seventy blows upon the body, and upon all the race
threads.summary_md:
Yahuah Elohim (the Lord God) is angry, and says to Adam: *In that thou hast left behind my commandment and hast not kept my word* (Adam and Eve 77:1). The consequence is named at once: *seventy blows* (Adam and Eve 77:1) on every limb, and on all the race. The shape of it is not new. In the covenant, the judgement for leaving the word falls on the one who left it and on his seed: *Then Yahuah (LORD) will make thy plagues wonderful, and the plagues of thy seed, even great plagues, and of long continuance, and sore sicknesses, and of long continuance.* (Deuteronomy 28:59)

Paul states the reach of the first failure in a single sentence: *Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned:* (Romans 5:12) It ain't new that one man's act reaches his house. The Torah is not the curse here; the judgement is. The commandment was given, it was left, and the consequence came, which is the whole movement of Deuteronomy 28. This book counts the blows; the canon only says the plagues were sore, and long, and that they touched the seed.

threads.title: Six days, and herbs of fragrance
threads.summary_md:
Michael sends Seth back to his father: *the time of his life is fulfilled. Six days hence, his soul shall go off his body* (Adam and Eve 86:1). The span is the one Moses closes the book of Adam's life with: *And all the days that Adam lived were nine hundred and thirty years: and he died.* (Genesis 5:5) The man who was told in the day thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die lives long, and then he dies, and the number is written down.

Eve and Seth return from the gates of paradise without the oil, carrying *herbs of fragrance, i.e. nard and crocus and calamus and cinnamon* (Adam and Eve 86:2). Those are four names from the Song: *Spikenard and saffron; calamus and cinnamon, with all trees of frankincense; myrrh and aloes, with all the chief spices:* (Song of Solomon 4:14) It ain't new that the spices of the garden were meant for the living to give each other. What they bring is what can be had outside, and the ending of the matter is on its way. The oil is not given now, as Michael said; the herbs are given, and the six days begin.

threads.title: A great plague for all our generations
threads.summary_md:
Seth and his mother come back to Adam and tell him the beast bit Seth. Adam, in his sickness, hears it as the fall again: *A great plague hast thou brought upon us, transgression and sin for all our generations* (Adam and Eve 87:1). He even says what his children will say: they will curse them for the evils of the beginning. The reach is real. Paul writes it without softening: *For as in Adam all die, even so in Messiah (Christ) shall all be made alive.* (1 Corinthians 15:22)

The second half of the same verse is the answer this book does not reach here. And on the matter of the children's curse, Yahuah (the LORD) speaks through Ezekiel to a people who had a proverb of their own: *The soul that sinneth, it shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son: the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him.* (Ezekiel 18:20) It ain't new that sin spreads to the household and that each one is called to answer for his own. The grief of Adam is true, and the way out of it, in the canon, is the other half of that verse.

threads.title: Blessed art thou, O Yahuah, for pity on thy creature
threads.summary_md:
The sentence is short: *Blessed art thou, O Yahuah (Lord), for thou hast had pity on Thy creature* (Adam and Eve 90:1). It is the blessing of someone who has been spared something he did not earn. The psalmist knows the ground of it: *Yahuah (LORD) is good to all: and his tender mercies are over all his works.* (Psalm 145:9)

The same word of blessing is heard again at the dawn of the gospels, on the lips of Zechariah as his son John is born: *Blessed be Yahuah Elohim (the Lord God) of Yashar'el (Israel); for he hath visited and redeemed his people,* (Luke 1:68) It ain't new that the one who has been shown pity answers with blessing. This book puts it at the close of Adam's life; the canon puts it in the mouth of a priest at the beginning of a new visiting. The same Yahuah (the LORD) pities his creature at the first end and at the last.

members.member_note: Genesis 4:11 — *which hath opened her mouth to receive thy brother’s blood from thy hand.* The earth that opens her mouth for Abel's blood is the dream's mouth made plain.
1 Peter 5:8 — *your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour.* Adam's dread of the adversary is the apostle's warning given a household.
Genesis 3:22 — *lest he put forth his hand, and take also of the tree of life, and eat, and live for ever.* The fruit Seth offers to fetch is the tree Genesis says was guarded from the man.
Revelation 22:14 — *that they may have right to the tree of life.* The tree Seth would fetch for is given at the end to those who do his commandments.

Genesis 3:17 — *Because thou hast hearkened unto the voice of thy wife, and hast eaten of the tree, of which I commanded thee.* In Genesis the sentence falls on the man who ate, not only on the woman who gave.
Genesis 3:12 — *The woman whom thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I did eat.* The blame passed across the household in the garden is still being passed here.
Genesis 2:15 — *to dress it and to keep it.* The guarding of paradise in Eve's account is the keeping Genesis gives to the man.
Genesis 2:19 — *brought them unto Adam to see what he would call them.* Genesis puts the creatures before Adam; the division in Eve's account is not in Moses.
Genesis 3:1 — *Yea, hath Elohim (God) said, Ye shall not eat of every tree of the garden?.* The question the serpent put to the woman is the devil's plan spoken.
Revelation 12:9 — *that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan, which deceiveth the whole world.* The devil and the serpent in Eve's account are named together in Revelation.
Psalm 119:137 — *Righteous art thou, O Yahuah (LORD), and upright are thy judgments.* The angels' worship of a just judgement is the psalmist's confession.
Genesis 3:24 — *So he drove out the man.* The expulsion the angels carry out is the driving out Genesis records.
Deuteronomy 4:9 — *but teach them thy sons, and thy sons’ sons.* Eve's charge to her children's children is Moses' charge to Yashar'el (Israel).
Genesis 3:13 — *The serpent beguiled me, and I did eat.* Eve's whole account to her children is already in her one answer in the garden.
Psalm 148:3 — *Praise ye him, sun and moon: praise him, all ye stars of light.* The wonders before the throne are the sun and moon the psalm summons to praise.
Genesis 1:16 — *Elohim (God) made two great lights.* The lights Eve sees are the two great lights made on the fourth day.
Genesis 1:27 — *So Elohim (God) created man in his own image.* The angels' plea that he is Thine image is the creation word in Genesis.
Ezekiel 1:1 — *the heavens were opened, and I saw visions of Elohim (God).* The heavens opened over Eve and Seth are the heavens opened over Ezekiel.
Psalm 18:10 — *he rode upon a cherub, and did fly.* The cherubim on the winds are the cherub and wings of the wind in the psalm.
Genesis 4:25 — *Elohim (God), said she, hath appointed me another seed instead of Abel.* Seth born according to the appointment is Eve's word at his birth in Genesis.
Genesis 3:23 — *sent him forth from the garden of Eden, to till the ground from whence he was taken.* The sending forth in Genesis is where the booth and the mourning begin.
Joel 2:12 — *turn ye even to me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning.* The grief of the booth is the weeping Joel names as the road back.
Genesis 3:19 — *In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread.* Eve's hunger is the first meal of the sentence Genesis records.
Psalm 103:13 — *Like as a father pitieth his children, so Yahuah (LORD) pitieth them that fear him.* Eve's hope of pity is the fatherly pity the psalm promises.
Genesis 2:23 — *This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh.* Adam's refusal to touch his own flesh is the first word he spoke of Eve.
Genesis 2:24 — *and they shall be one flesh.* The two who must live on together are the one flesh Genesis names.
Ecclesiastes 5:4 — *When thou vowest a vow unto Elohim (God), defer not to pay it.* Eve's dread of unpaid promises is the Preacher's warning on vows.
Psalm 51:17 — *a broken and a contrite heart, O Elohim (God), thou wilt not despise.* The question of how much penitence is answered in the heart, not the labour.
Genesis 2:14 — *the name of the third river is Hiddekel.* The river Eve stands in is one of those that came out of Eden.
Matthew 3:6 — *And were baptized of him in Jordan, confessing their sins.* The Jordan where Adam stands is the river where the people came to confess.
2 Corinthians 11:14 — *Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light.* The devil's kindness to Eve is the disguise Paul names.
2 Timothy 2:26 — *recover themselves out of the snare of the devil.* Adam's word for being ensnared is Paul's word for the devil's snare.
James 4:7 — *Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.* Eve's cry against the devil is the beginning of the resisting James describes.
Zechariah 3:2 — *Yahuah (LORD) rebuke thee, O Satan.* The rebuke Eve gives is, in the prophet's vision, spoken by Yahuah (the LORD).
Ezekiel 28:16 — *thou hast sinned: therefore I will cast thee as profane out of the mountain of Elohim (God).* The casting out is, in the prophet, the answer to the cherub's own sin.
Luke 10:18 — *I beheld Satan as lightning fall from heaven.* The glory lost in the heavens is the fall Yahusha (Jesus) saw.
Genesis 1:26 — *Let us make man in our image, after our likeness.* The image Michael tells the angels to honour is the image of Genesis 1.
Revelation 22:9 — *See thou do it not: for I am thy fellowservant … worship Elohim (God).* The canon keeps worship for Elohim (God) alone, even before an angel.
Psalm 31:15 — *My times are in thy hand: deliver me from the hand of mine enemies.* Adam's prayer against the Adversary is David's prayer against his persecutors.
Psalm 69:1 — *Save me, O Elohim (God); for the waters are come in unto my soul.* The man standing in the Jordan prays what the psalmist prays in deep water.
Genesis 3:16 — *in sorrow thou shalt bring forth children.* Eve's pangs are the sorrow in childbearing named in the sentence.
John 16:21 — *A woman when she is in travail hath sorrow, because her hour is come.* The travail Eve cries from ends, as Yahusha (Jesus) says, in a child born.
Genesis 4:2 — *And Abel was a keeper of sheep, but Cain was a tiller of the ground.* The brothers who stayed together are named by the work that divided them.
Genesis 4:10 — *the voice of thy brother’s blood crieth unto me from the ground.* The blood Eve sees in a vision is the blood that cries from the ground.
Genesis 4:9 — *And he said, I know not: Am I my brother’s keeper?* Adam keeping the boys apart is the keeping that Cain refused.
Psalm 51:11 — *Cast me not away from thy presence.* Adam's prayer not to be cast out is David's prayer in the psalm.
Isaiah 66:22 — *so shall your seed and your name remain.* The seed that is not cut off in this book is the seed that remains in Isaiah.
Psalm 36:9 — *For with thee is the fountain of life: in thy light shall we see light.* Adam's praise of the Light and the Living Life is the psalm's fountain and light.
Psalm 90:2 — *even from everlasting to everlasting, thou art Elohim (God).* Adam's eternal and supreme Elohim (God) is the everlasting Elohim (God) of the psalm.
Joshua 7:6 — *and put dust upon their heads.* Seth's dust on his head is the gesture of Joshua and the elders at the ark.
Psalm 38:3 — *There is no soundness in my flesh because of thine anger.* The pain Adam describes to Seth is the pain the psalmist ties to sin.
Genesis 2:17 — *in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die.* Adam's prohibition is the commandment of Genesis with its penalty.
Genesis 2:9 — *the tree of life also in the midst of the garden, and the tree of knowledge of good and evil.* The tree in the midst of paradise is the tree Moses places next to the tree of life.
Deuteronomy 28:59 — *the plagues of thy seed, even great plagues.* The blows laid on the body and on the race are the plagues on the seed in Moses.
Romans 5:12 — *as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin.* What Adam says falls on all his race is what Paul says passed upon all men.
2 Samuel 24:17 — *Lo, I have sinned, and I have done wickedly.* Eve's asking to take the pain is David's asking to take the stroke.
Galatians 6:2 — *Bear ye one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Messiah (Christ).* Eve asking for a part of Adam's pain is a burden borne for another.
Numbers 22:28 — *Yahuah (LORD) opened the mouth of the ass.* The speaking beast has its one plain precedent in Balaam's ass.
Genesis 9:2 — *And the fear of you and the dread of you shall be upon every beast of the earth.* The beasts' malice against Eve is the strain between man and beast in Genesis.
James 5:14 — *anointing him with oil in the name of Yahuah (Lord).* The oil sought for the sick Adam is the oil of anointing James names.
Psalm 103:3 — *Who forgiveth all thine iniquities; who healeth all thy diseases.* What the mourners beg for is what the psalm says Yahuah (the LORD) does.
Revelation 22:2 — *the leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations.* The tree of mercy withheld now is the tree of life at the end.
Habakkuk 2:3 — *though it tarry, wait for it; because it will surely come.* The oil that waits for the end is the vision that waits for its time.
Genesis 5:5 — *all the days that Adam lived were nine hundred and thirty years: and he died.* The fulfilled life Michael speaks of is the nine hundred and thirty years of Genesis.
Song of Solomon 4:14 — *Spikenard and saffron; calamus and cinnamon.* The four herbs they carry home are four spices of the Song's garden.
1 Corinthians 15:22 — *For as in Adam all die, even so in Messiah (Christ) shall all be made alive.* Adam's grief over the reach of the fall is answered in Paul by a reach of life.
Ezekiel 18:20 — *The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father.* The children's complaint against their parents is met by Ezekiel's word on whose sin is whose.
Psalm 145:9 — *his tender mercies are over all his works.* The blessing for pity on the creature rests on the mercy over all his works.
Luke 1:68 — *for he hath visited and redeemed his people.* Adam's blessing for pity is Zechariah's blessing for a visit of redemption.
